opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we ran into a lot in practice. When you train a generator on a narrow, curated domain, say, aligned faces or a single category of objects, you can get remarkably high-quality results. The model has a much easier job, because the distribution is tight, and it can really nail the fine details. That's a big part of why the early GAN results on faces looked so stunning.

The limitation is that the model only knows that world. It hasn't seen enough variation to understand how things compose, how lighting behaves across different scenes, or how objects relate to each other. So as soon as you push it slightly outside that distribution, a face at an unusual angle, an occlusion, a background it hasn't seen, things degrade quickly. You get artifacts, or the model just snaps back to the average of what it knows.

There's also a subtler issue around "good" images specifically. If you only train on clean, well-composed, professionally shot photos, you bake in an aesthetic bias. That might be what you want for some products, but it limits diversity, and it can also limit the model's understanding of the visual world, because a lot of what helps a model generalize comes from the messy, imperfect data.

What we've seen with the larger models is that training broadly first, on huge, diverse, noisy data, gives you a strong general prior, and then you can fine-tune or filter toward quality afterward. That tends to beat training only on narrow, curated data from the start. So I'd say narrow domains are great for depth and fidelity, but breadth is what gives you robustness and flexibility, and the best results so far come from combining the two.

r001.rationale: The response says a generator trained on a narrow, curated domain degrades when pushed outside that distribution, producing artifacts or reverting to familiar averages.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that when you train a generative model on a curated set of good images from one narrow domain, you're really teaching it the distribution of that domain, and that's both the strength and the limit. It works beautifully as long as what you want to generate stays inside that distribution. If you train on, say, high-quality landscape photographs, you'll get very convincing landscapes.

But a couple of things break down. The first is coverage. A narrow dataset by definition has holes in it, and the model has no way of knowing what sits in those holes. It'll either hallucinate something plausible-looking but wrong, or it'll just collapse toward the modes it saw most often. So you lose diversity, and you lose the long tail, which is often the part that's actually interesting.

The second thing is that "good" is a judgment call baked in at dataset construction time. You've essentially frozen an aesthetic or a quality criterion into the model, and the model can't move beyond it. If your notion of good shifts, or if a user wants something that your curators would have filtered out, you're stuck. The model doesn't understand why those images were good, it just knows they're what exists.

And the third limit, which I think is underappreciated, is compositionality. Narrow-domain models tend not to learn concepts that transfer. A model trained only on faces doesn't learn much about lighting or geometry in a general way that would help it with, say, hands or outdoor scenes. Whereas models trained on broad, messy data, even with a lot of low-quality examples, pick up a kind of general visual knowledge that lets you then steer or fine-tune them toward a specific domain. So in practice I've come to see the narrow, curated approach as more of a finishing step than a foundation. You want the breadth first, and then you can use the good narrow data to shape the output, rather than relying on it to teach the model about images in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow-domain models work well inside their training distribution but have coverage gaps and tend not to learn concepts that transfer, illustrating that they may not generate good images beyond the domain.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key distinction is between image quality and coverage. You can have a dataset of really beautiful images, but if they all come from a narrow domain, the model has relatively little evidence about anything outside that domain. It might produce very convincing results for things that look like its training data, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle a new subject or a new combination of concepts.

And even within that domain, you have to ask whether it’s capturing the full range of variation or just learning a few common patterns. So training on good images can help, but it doesn’t by itself solve the generalization problem. The question is: what do you want the generator to be able to do, and does the data actually support that?

r001.rationale: The response says that a narrow-domain dataset gives the model little evidence about subjects outside that domain, so convincing results on familiar data do not ensure it can handle new subjects or combinations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the limitation is that “good” is always relative to the domain. If you train on a very narrow set of images, the model can get quite good at producing things that look like that set. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it understands what makes an image good, or that it can carry that judgment over to a different setting.

And there’s a coverage issue. Even within that domain, the training images may only show a small portion of what you’d want to generate. So you can get very convincing results near the examples you’ve given it, but when you ask for a new composition or an unusual combination of elements, you start to see the limits. Visual quality and the ability to generalize are related, but they’re not the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response says that a model trained on a narrow set may not carry its judgment of image quality to a different setting, and describes limits when generating beyond the examples.
